title: With modern AI coding tools making development much easier, what will make developers valuable in the future?
author: Cold-Ruin-1017
selftext:
AI coding tools are getting really powerful now. Many IDEs can read the whole project, generate features, fix bugs, write tests, and explain the code. Because of that, a lot of the actual coding work feels much easier than before.

In many cases the workflow feels like this:

1. Understand the problem
2. Give the AI the right context or prompt
3. Review the generated code
4. Refactor or adjust parts if needed

Because of this, it sometimes feels like a big part of the traditional coding effort is reduced.

So my question is: what will actually make developers valuable going forward?

If AI can generate most of the code, explain it, and help debug it, why would companies still pay high salaries for developers? What are we really bringing to the table that AI plus a reasonably technical person couldn’t do?

I’m a frontend / React developer and I’m trying to understand how the role of developers might evolve as these tools become more common.

Curious how other engineers see this.
What skills or abilities do you think will actually differentiate developers in the next few years?

comments.author: drnktgr
comments.body: The idea guy. The influencer guy.

comments.author: count023
comments.body:
what will make the developer better is knowing patterns and processes more than the languages. 

You know your command pattern and where to apply it? factory pattern? separate of data planes, all that stuff.

Developers will evolve more into a designer/orchestrator type role where you wont have to write line by line, because you'll map your code and functions out and have te AI write the lines up based on your lines.

replies.author: ProclarushTaonasA
replies.body: Yeah. AI Is a Tool. You still need to understand what you want the Programm to do, and to convey it to the AI. Most of the criticism of AI comes from the AI slop, which comes from people trying to use AI without knowing how to use it correctly. You cant Just Tell an AI to make "Art", you can Tell it to make a Pictures featuring xyz, wether that results in Art or Not is Up to Debate.

replies.author: Crawling_Hustler
replies.body:
U forget that AI knows usage of patterns based on use cases better than humans. I mean if they r common ones like command, factory, or even behavior trees,etc. 

U give it the use case and ur requirements and it can give u list of viable patterns along with their pros and cons. The only skill here is to tell your requirements.

replies.author: count023
replies.body:
no, i'm aware of it, but it doesnt have hte instinctive leap to properly integrate them. you will see a lot of times that you tell it to do something, it'll mix things together, for instance, it might hard code values between classes, or create multiple singletons rather than reuse hte one that's there as for an FSM, or it might mix and match paterns in an inefficient way. Knowing OOP, data handling rules, best practices and patterns means you can look at hte AI's output and go, "hey, that's not right, x y and z are wrong, go back and fix it" and then it can. 

That's what seperates the slop from the actual accelerated dev work.

replies.author: Crawling_Hustler
replies.body:
Yes, i agree with ur last part . Having knowledge is required to know if AI is doing mistakes. But i think its temporary issue and AI will decrease mistakes a lot in few years (one dev with basic knowledge can look into multiple areas while AI does 95% of job). 

Like u said, AI making duplicate files, not reusing existing variables,  files, etc is common issue. 
Which, is already solved by AI agents with large context capacity. These agent also makes documentation which it uses to easily find existing helper files, common Manager or utility files ,etc. So, it wont duplicate and remake smth that already exists. 

It even asks you if u want AI to remake separate file or reuse it. This issue was due to lack of context which is almost (>90%) fixed.

replies.author: daddywookie
replies.body:
As a non-coder I’m using a no-code game engine already. I still need to understand a lot about how to architect my game, the design aspects, how I want to manage and balance it, what is fun, what looks good… 

The writing of the code is the part which can be abstracted ever higher. Compiled languages might end up just being another step along this road.

comments.author: austinthrowaway4949
comments.body: I think you need to scale your ambition, your idea of what you can accomplish. If AI makes your existing workload trivial then you have to accept that it's over, it's time to take on larger, more difficult projects where you are the architect, the engineering manager... and your "employees" are essentially genius coders but overly confident, overly agreeable, lacking any persistent memory or real world experience. There will be a huge gap between those who just tell AI to do their job and get lazy, vs those who build things they would have never had the time/resources to build pre-AI.

comments.author: tomqmasters
comments.body: Coding already was the most automated job in the world.  If you think AI is a big deal wait until you find out about unit testing.  Way more valuable.

comments.author: corysama
comments.body: Every day we stray further from [Mel.](https://users.cs.utah.edu/~elb/folklore/mel.html)

comments.author: bangbreakfast
comments.body:
Developer value always comes in three forms: writing code, solving complex business problems, and debugging/performance engineering. 

AI makes writing code cheap. Gone are the days of writing hundreds of lines of code so instead value now shifts on to the other areas. AI can help assist in these area but it still requires expertise in order to achieve desired results. 

I would like to mention that AI still tends to build a lot of bloated code at times. This is very costly if not monitored correctly….which leads me to what i think is the most valuable now more than ever debugging and performance engineering.

comments.author: SovereignLG
comments.body:
Great question. Although it's true that with the continued advancement of AI tech for coding, the effort to code is reduced, what we're seeing is the continued need for oversight/orchestration of AI Agents. 

I'm sure the technology will get to the place where it could likely orchestrate itself to a high degree of confidence, but till then, there's still need for humans who can create the proper context for agents to actually do their work effectively. I'm seeing this called "harness engineering". 

And at the end of the day, someone who still has a developer experience and mindset would be more successful over an individual with a different skill set in my opinion.

comments.author: Aware-Source6313
comments.body:
Talking more about swe than game dev? A lot of gamedev is beyond functional code. It's art/entertainment; the deliverable is an experience rather than (as it is for most swe jobs) a business outcome. 

For enterprise swe, architecture/systems knowledge may still be valuable for a while. Otherwise just understanding well the intersection of the business with the technology rather than being purely siloed in the tech (already/always valuable). Ability to prioritize technical efforts. Ability to communicate and be accountable. 

All of this remains even assuming coding tools reach technically at the level of the best SWE,  but it still produces mistakes, bad design, bad architecture, sycophantic to your suggestions, misses or writes bugs, and hallucinates. 

All of these can get better but if not eliminated you will need someone that at least moderately understands the tech and can, at least with ai assistance, troubleshoot complex issues that the ai missed. In the interim as well, being able to leverage AI tools, and build and utilize agentic systems efficiently will be potentially very valuable, until the models are so good that orchestration is easy and these skill lose value.

comments.author: Stunning_Algae_9065
comments.body:
I think what will make developers valuable is still the ability to understand systems and solve problems, not just write syntax. AI can generate code pretty well, but deciding *what should actually be built*, how different parts of a system interact, and catching subtle logic issues is still a human job.

In our team we’ve noticed that a lot of the time goes into reviewing changes, debugging weird edge cases, and making sure a fix in one place doesn’t break something else. AI helps speed things up, but someone still needs to understand the whole system.

That’s why tools that help with debugging and PR reviews are becoming interesting too, not just code generation ))

comments.author: Admirable_Gazelle453
comments.body: It seems like value is shifting toward problem framing, system design, and making tradeoffs rather than just writing code, since AI still needs strong direction. Even tools like Horizons make building easier, but knowing what to build and why is still the real edge, and it stays affordable with vibecodersnest discount code
